lesson.title: The Body's Outgoing Commands
lesson.summary: Motor, or efferent, neurons carry commands from the central nervous system out to muscles and glands, converting neural decisions into the muscle contractions that produce actual movement.
lesson.body:
If sensory neurons are the nervous system's incoming messengers, motor neurons are its outgoing commands. Also called efferent neurons, they carry signals away from the central nervous system out to the muscles and glands that actually produce a physical response. The direction is the mirror image of the sensory neurons covered earlier: efferent means away from the brain and spinal cord, not toward it.

A typical motor neuron has its cell body located within the central nervous system, in the ventral, or front-facing, gray matter of the spinal cord or within specific nuclei of the brainstem. From there, a single long axon extends outward, sometimes for a considerable distance, all the way to a muscle fiber. At its end, the axon forms a specialized connection called the neuromuscular junction, where it releases the neurotransmitter acetylcholine directly onto the muscle, triggering the muscle fiber to contract.

Motor neurons actually come in two broad categories. Upper motor neurons originate in the motor cortex and descend through the brainstem and spinal cord, carrying voluntary commands downward, while lower motor neurons are the ones described above, with cell bodies in the spinal cord or brainstem and axons that leave the central nervous system to reach muscle directly. Only the lower motor neuron actually forms the neuromuscular junction and triggers contraction, but it typically will not fire unless it receives enough input from upper motor neurons or from local spinal reflex circuits.

Motor neurons are the final link that connects the somatic nervous system's decisions, whether deliberate or reflexive, to actual movement. Every skeletal muscle contraction, from lifting a fork to sprinting, ultimately depends on motor neurons delivering the command to the correct muscle fibers at the correct time.

Return once more to the example of the hand withdrawn from a hot stove. After sensory neurons detect the heat and neurons in the spinal cord process the signal, it is a motor neuron that carries the final command out to the muscles of the arm, triggering the rapid contraction that pulls the hand away, all within a fraction of a second and without waiting for the brain to weigh in.

Because individual motor neurons obey the all-or-none principle, meaning each one either fires completely or not at all, the nervous system produces smooth, graded muscle contractions not by making single neurons fire harder, but by adjusting how many motor neurons fire and how rapidly they fire in sequence. A gentle grip recruits relatively few motor units firing at a modest rate, while a powerful grip recruits many more motor units firing rapidly, a principle that becomes clearer once the all-or-none rule itself is examined directly. Diseases that damage motor neurons, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, show just how essential this pathway is: as motor neurons degenerate, the muscles they once controlled gradually lose the ability to contract, even though the muscle tissue itself remains intact.
